intro: Foundations of International Law. Unit eight: international organizations, part two — the United Nations, and the organizations based in Vienna.

slides.7: Recommendations are not nothing. Set binding decisions and non-binding recommendations against each other, and the recommendations turn out to be the more interesting half. They vary in authority but have legal effects nonetheless: a member must consider a recommendation in good faith, and conduct that conforms to it benefits from a presumption of legality. They can also be catalysts — for custom, by evidencing opinio iuris, and for treaties — and they support arguments before courts. Binding decisions, by contrast, are rare and mostly concern internal organizational regulation; the exceptions are the Security Council, which created the Yugoslavia and Rwanda tribunals, and European Union law.
slides.8: The Chagos Advisory Opinion. The material gives only a title, a photograph of a Chagossian protester holding a sign reading 'The UK took our island home for a US Air Base', and a map placing the Chagos Islands in the middle of the Indian Ocean. The advisory opinion of 2019 held that the decolonization of Mauritius had not been lawfully completed, because the Chagos Archipelago was detached before independence, and that the United Kingdom is under an obligation to end its administration as rapidly as possible. That reasoning is not in the material itself, so verify it against the lecture. It appears here as an example of the General Assembly using its power to request advisory opinions.
slides.15: What the Economic and Social Council is for — six functions. Promoting a higher standard of living, full employment, and economic and social progress. Solving international economic, social and health problems. International cooperation in culture and education. Strengthening global respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. And making recommendations and programmes for member states and the United Nations system. Then comes the figure that surprises people: roughly seventy per cent of the personnel and financial resources of the United Nations sit in this broad mandate, not in the peace and security work.
slides.23: Vienna organizations, second group: the Test-Ban Treaty Organization and the OSCE. The CTBTO Preparatory Commission, in Vienna since 1997, works to obtain ratifications and signatures of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty of 1996, and operates a global monitoring system of seismic, hydroacoustic and infrasound measurements. Note that it is still a preparatory commission, because the treaty has not entered into force. The OSCE, in Vienna since 1995, succeeded the CSCE as a platform between East and West; and its character as an international organization is disputed, because it was never founded by a treaty.
slides.24: Vienna organizations, third group: UNIDO and OPEC. UNIDO, the United Nations Industrial Development Organization, founded in 1966 and in Vienna from 1967, works on poverty reduction through productive capacity, trade capacity building, and energy and environment. OPEC, founded in 1960 and in Vienna since 1965, is described with unusual frankness as an international oil cartel that sets production quotas — a reminder that an international organization need not pursue a public-interest purpose in order to be one.
slides.25: A picture of OPEC, with nothing further said about it.
slides.26: The Vienna International Centre again — the United Nations complex in Vienna, the same one as in the previous unit.
slides.27: What the organizations are worth to Austria. A 2020 study by Jan Kluge and Alexander Schnabl, commissioned by the Austrian Ministry for European and International Affairs, on the economic effects of international organizations in Austria. It is the practical answer to why a state competes to host organizations: the headquarters agreement costs privileges and immunities, and buys employment and international standing.
